1. Introduction

1.1 What is a place-based business case (PBBC)?

A place-based business case (PBBC) is a tool for stakeholders in local, regional, devolved and central government to develop and agree:

A shared, evidence-based understanding of a place, including its challenges and opportunities

A coherent set of objectives for that place

A package of interventions most likely to achieve those objectives

1.2 What does a PBBC do?

A PBBC provides a strategic framework for coordinating investment in a place. In doing so, it can reduce duplication and accelerate subsequent business case processes.

Achieving the objectives of a place will often require more than a single project or programme. Projects and programmes within a place can also interact in ways that materially affect whether those objectives are achieved.

A core purpose of a PBBC is therefore to identify a ‘package’ of interventions that work together to achieve the objectives of a place. A package can include public and private investment, alongside regulatory changes or other measures.

1.3 Why use a PBBC?

The authority, funding and capability needed to develop and deliver a package of interventions are often spread across different levels of government. Without effective coordination, organisations risk making decisions in isolation, missing opportunities to align investment and failing to take account of different priorities for a place.

A PBBC supports better, more joined-up decision making to achieve the objectives of a place. A PBBC may be particularly useful where there is a need to:

Coordinate new and existing investment where no effective mechanism already exists

Identify the optimal mix of interventions needed to achieve the objectives of a place, especially where these are transformational

Respond collectively to significant economic, social or environmental challenges that require a coordinated place-based response

A PBBC is unlikely to add value where a single project or programme can achieve the objectives, or where there is limited opportunity for interventions to interact or contribute to shared place-based outcomes. In these circumstances, conventional project or programme business cases will usually be more appropriate.

A PBBC does not guarantee funding. Nor does it change the responsibilities of public bodies for making investment decisions within their respective remits.

1.4 Who is this guidance for?

Any public sector organisation can use this guidance to develop a PBBC. This guidance is also for public, private and third sector organisations invited to collaborate on a PBBC.

Developing a PBBC is voluntary. This guidance does not oblige any organisation to initiate, develop or collaborate on a PBBC.

1.5 How is this guidance structured?

This guidance sets out the process for developing a PBBC. In summary:

Chapters 1 and 2 set out the purpose and structure of a PBBC and how it fits within existing processes, including how it supports decision making and how it can help progress individual project and programme business cases

Chapters 3 to 7 set out how to develop a PBBC

Annex A sets out how social cost-benefit analysis can be incorporated into PBBCs

This guidance uses the following terms throughout:

Place: The area to which the objectives of the PBBC relate

Partners: The local, regional, devolved and central government bodies, other public sector organisations, and private and third sector organisations involved in developing a PBBC

Practitioners: A generic term referring to the individuals involved in developing a PBBC

2. Developing and approving a PBBC

2.1 Introduction

Like any business case, a PBBC brings together the evidence needed to support good decisions. This chapter explains how a PBBC fits with existing business case and spending processes, and then how to structure a PBBC.

2.2 Who should initiate a PBBC and when?

Any public sector organisation can use this guidance to initiate a PBBC. Local authorities and strategic authorities are most likely to initiate a PBBC given their role in identifying and pursuing objectives for their place. There is no prescribed point at which to initiate one, although Chapter 1 sets out circumstances where a PBBC may be particularly useful. Figure 1 shows the steps from identifying a place-based opportunity or challenge to deciding to develop a PBBC.

Figure 1. Deciding when to develop a PBBC

This guidance refers to the partner that chooses to develop a PBBC as the ‘initiating partner’. Where a UK government department is the initiating partner, it must always invite the support and involvement of the relevant local, regional and devolved governments.

2.3 How should partners work together?

The initiating partner is responsible for bringing partners together to agree roles, responsibilities, governance arrangements and ways of working at the outset.

The initiating partner should identify and engage organisations that may need to:

Explore and assess interventions that might make up the package

Fund interventions within the package

Approve interventions within the package

Support the delivery of interventions within the package

Early engagement helps partners develop a shared understanding of the place and its priorities, identify dependencies and build agreement around the emerging package.

Partners should develop the PBBC together. One organisation should not develop a PBBC independently and present it to others as a completed proposal. The PBBC should reflect a shared assessment of the place’s challenges, opportunities and priorities. This ongoing collaboration will be particularly important when partners seek approval for the PBBC.

Partners developing a PBBC in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland should engage the relevant devolved government on any potential interventions in devolved policy areas.

7.5 Action 18: Develop a benefits realisation and evaluation plan

Practitioners should develop a high-level benefits realisation and evaluation plan for the preferred package. This should explain how partners will track and manage the intended place-based outcomes during delivery and how interventions detailed in the PBBC will be evaluated. This should draw directly on the objectives and theory of change in the strategic case.

Practitioners should evaluate individual projects and programmes in line with the Magenta Book. Practitioners should also plan how they will evaluate the overall results of the package of interventions in the PBBC. This is important to ensure that lessons can be learned about how different interventions work together in practice, and what results they do, or do not, achieve collectively.

Planning for evaluation should begin at the outset, to ensure that appropriate plans can be put in place early to capture relevant data, design suitable methods and engage with stakeholders.

The overall place-based evaluation should assess whether the package achieved the objectives set out in the strategic case, whether it alleviated the binding constraints set out in the economic case, and whether the expected benefits were realised.

Practitioners can seek further guidance on benefits realisation and evaluation from resources including the:

Magenta Book, which contains guidance on evaluation approaches

Guidance on developing business cases, which contains guidance on how to plan monitoring and evaluation within standard business cases

Teal Book (Chapters 2 and 19), which provides more information about planning for evaluation alongside benefits management activities

8. Annex A: Social cost-benefit analysis in a PBBC

EPA will normally provide sufficient evidence to assess the potential of shortlisted packages. A PBBC does not therefore always need package-level CBA.

Practitioners may use CBA to supplement EPA, or as the primary basis for selecting a preferred package following Action 9, where partners agree that this would materially support decisions or subsequent programme, project or funding approvals.

The steps below show how practitioners can apply CBA to shortlisted packages following Action 9.

8.1 Step 1: Assess costs and benefits of individual interventions

Practitioners should assess the monetisable costs and benefits of each intervention contained within the shortlisted packages in line with the Green Book. This step should focus on impacts within the outcome area defined in the strategic case.

Practitioners should first assess each intervention on a standalone basis, assuming that the other interventions in the package are not delivered. This provides a baseline for assessing the additional effects of interventions working together in subsequent steps.

Where appropriate, practitioners should calculate the relevant summary metrics for each intervention, including the net present social value (NPSV) and the benefit-cost ratio (BCR). They should also identify and describe material costs and benefits that cannot be monetised.

8.2 Step 2: Assess costs and benefits of intervention packages

Practitioners should assess the monetisable costs and benefits of each shortlisted package within the outcome area. This assessment should assume that all interventions within the package are delivered.

Practitioners should assess whether delivering interventions together changes their costs and benefits. This should capture any additional benefits or costs that arise from interactions between interventions.

When an intervention is already under way, practitioners should exclude costs and benefits that would arise anyway, while including any additional effects that result from delivering it alongside other interventions in the package.

Where the evidence allows, practitioners should estimate the additional monetisable value created by interactions between interventions. This can be assessed by comparing the NPSV of the complete package with the sum of the standalone NPSVs calculated in Step 1:

Package synergy = NPSV of package − sum of standalone intervention NPSVs

Where interactions cannot be robustly monetised, practitioners should quantify them in non-monetary terms where possible or describe their expected effects.

Practitioners should calculate the relevant summary metrics for each shortlisted package.

8.3 Step 3: Assess costs and benefits at the UK level

Practitioners should assess the costs and benefits of each shortlisted package from a UK-wide perspective. This should establish the net social value of each package to the UK as a whole.

Practitioners should adjust the analysis from Step 2 to account for displacement, substitution, leakage and other relevant effects. This should distinguish between benefits experienced within the outcome area and benefits that are additional to the UK as a whole.

When assessing employment impacts at the UK level, practitioners should generally assume that proposals do not bring about an increase in national labour supply. This is known as the principle of full displacement of jobs. There may, however, be exceptional circumstances where the assumption of full displacement of jobs does not hold in a local economy, and practitioners may credibly assume that their proposal will increase labour supply. If practitioners assume that their proposal will increase labour supply, this must be accompanied by transparent reasoning and compelling evidence. Decision makers should be alert to this assumption. Practitioners should make sure this social benefit is carefully monitored and evaluated to inform future decision making.

There is a credible link between weaker inputs and poorer economic outcomes: Practitioners should consider whether changes in the severity of the constraint, either over time or across otherwise comparable parts of the place, are associated with changes in the outcome it is expected to affect. If a potential constraint is important, a more severe constraint should generally be associated with a poorer outcome, and vice versa. Practitioners should also consider alternative explanations, including whether poorer economic outcomes could themselves be contributing to the apparent constraint.

Example: Action 6

Practitioners distinguished between binding and secondary constraints in Middlemarch.

Constraint Type Description

Low technical skills Binding Vacancy data and employer evidence consistently indicate a shortage of technical skills relative to employer demand. Evidence shows a relationship between access to these skills and firms’ ability to improve productivity, particularly in advanced manufacturing and digital sectors.

Limited housing supply Binding Housing supply has not kept pace with demand, while affordability and availability indicators suggest difficulties accommodating additional workers. A shortage of housing constrains the labour supply and makes it harder to attract new residents and businesses.

Poor rail connectivity Secondary Journey times and service frequencies indicate relatively weak access to employment opportunities and surrounding labour markets. However, current evidence suggests that skills and housing constraints are more immediate limits on firms’ ability to recruit and expand, so improved rail connectivity is unlikely to have a material impact until those binding constraints are addressed.

Poor health outcomes Secondary Employment data indicates that ill health is preventing some residents from accessing employment. However, the number affected is small relative to the overall population, so addressing this would not meaningfully alter overall productivity.

Energy network capacity Secondary There are limits to energy capacity for large businesses, but current evidence does not indicate that this is materially constraining existing or expected economic activity.

4.4 Action 7: Identify appropriate comparators and estimate the economic potential of the place

Economic potential is the gap between:

The expected performance of the place under the BAU

The performance the place could realistically achieve if the binding constraints were eased

Practitioners should use ‘comparators’ to identify the scale of this potential. These are benchmarks used to help practitioners understand what the place could achieve, to inform the choice of preferred package.

Figure 3 sets out the different types of comparator. Practitioners must use a range of comparators, including national and regional averages, as well as two or three similar UK places. Practitioners may also use international comparators where this is justifiable and useful.

Figure 3. Types of comparator

Practitioners should select comparators:

Consistently and transparently: They should provide a clear rationale and avoid selective benchmarking simply to justify a predetermined package or intervention

Using statistical analysis and judgement: They should identify places that have sufficiently similar economic, demographic and geographic characteristics to provide meaningful comparison

Practitioners should use relevant indicators that may include rural-urban classification, levels of deprivation, labour market conditions, industrial structure, population profile and wider economic context.

Where possible, practitioners should use comparators that have achieved stronger outcomes from a sufficiently similar starting point. This will provide stretching but plausible benchmarks for improvement.

Example: Action 7 (identifying appropriate comparators)

The comparator selection process for Middlemarch focused on places that had experienced similar economic transitions and had successfully improved technical skills and housing over time.

Practitioners used the Office for National Statistics (ONS) statistical nearest neighbour methodology to help identify some suitable comparators in the UK. They also identified an international comparator, and regional and national averages.

Comparator Type Rationale

Northport UK place A former agricultural and manufacturing town with a similar population size and industrial structure to Middlemarch.

Westford UK place A town that successfully improved productivity by investing in technical skills provision and apprenticeships. Previously had similar issues to Middlemarch.

Riverton UK place A town with a similar demographic and industrial structure to Middlemarch that experienced significant growth following housing and road upgrades.

Bellacosta International comparator A medium-sized European town that transitioned from an agricultural economy towards advanced manufacturing and logistics following major housing investment.

Regional GVA and employment Regional average High-level benchmark against broader economic performance.

National GVA and employment National average High-level benchmark against broader economic performance at the national level.

Practitioners should set out how each comparator performs relative to the place in terms of the metrics they used when establishing the binding constraints. For example, when comparing Middlemarch with Westford, practitioners might provide a breakdown of population by qualification level for each place.
